title: The Nokia ringtone
hook: The famous Nokia ringtone is a few bars of a Spanish guitar waltz from 1902.
peek: Before it rang in billions of pockets, the Nokia tune was part of Gran Vals, a solo guitar piece by Francisco Tárrega. Nokia picked a short phrase from it in the 1990s and made it a global sound.
lede: The four-bar phrase that rang from Nokia phones around the world was not written for a phone. It comes from Gran Vals, a waltz for solo guitar by the Spanish composer Francisco Tárrega, from 1902. Nokia lifted a short passage from it in the early 1990s, and it became one of the most recognised tunes on the planet.

bullets.text: Tárrega was a guitarist and composer from Spain, often credited with helping the classical guitar become a serious concert instrument. His best-known piece is Recuerdos de la Alhambra. Gran Vals is a light, playful work by comparison.
The phrase appeared as a ringtone called Grande Valse on the Nokia 2110, released in 1994. As the phones spread it was renamed Nokia Tune, and it became the default sound on many models.

At its peak Nokia estimated the tune was heard about 1.8 billion times a day, or roughly 20,000 times a second. That is a company estimate, but it makes the phrase a strong candidate for the most-played piece of music ever.

Nokia kept the melody as its sonic logo and released new arrangements over the years, in styles from soft piano to dance music. Because the original is over a century old, Tárrega's waltz itself is in the public domain.
